sweep_summary: Mafea/Mavea (mafe1237) is not in the catalog. The sole works with stress in the title (Glottolog 524313, Zawaydeh et al. 2002 on Arabic rhythm) is a false Glottolog language tag - the reference record itself says 'computerized assignment from discovering' - and is irrelevant. The best first-hand stress statement is already held by the project and was re-read: Guérin & Aoyama 2009 (JIPA Illustration, p. 258): predominantly penultimate primary stress, non-phonemic, secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward, with two hedged exceptions (closed-final lexemes analysed as underlyingly penultimate; final stress on some disyllabic verbs in serial constructions); length non-phonemic. Copy Guérin 2011 A Grammar of Mavea (UHP/De Gruyter) has a section 2.3 'Word Stress' (p. 28) with 2.3.1 'Exceptions to penultimate stress' (p. 29) per the open JCU front-matter PDF (saved), but the body is paywalled (doi:10.1515/9780824837068-003); medium priority to acquire for the fuller statement. Crossref, UH ScholarSpace and archive.org queries yielded no further open sources. If Mafea were added to the catalog it would code as penultimate (quantity-insensitive, with secondary alternation), citing Guérin & Aoyama 2009 p. 258.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive; length is not phonemic, p. 256), non-contrastive and recomputed after suffixation (patu 'head' → patu-ira 'their head'). Secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the primary. The authors treat closed-final cases like [taˈm̼am] 'your father' as underlyingly penultimate (the lost POc *mu vowel of the 2SG possessive suffix still counts as a syllable), corroborated by sileti ~ [siˈleːt] 'worm' keeping penultimate stress after final-vowel deletion; a reviewer's weight-based alternative (closed final syllable always stressed) is recorded in fn. 14 but not adopted. Final stress on some disyllabic verbs (e.g. [moˈsi] 'he goes down') is attributed to serial-verb-construction phrasing and flagged as needing validation, with a comparison to Lewo (Early 1994: 68).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress falls on every second syllable to the left of the syllable receiving primary stress' (p. 258), e.g. [ˌpatuˈiːra] 'their head', [taˌmanaˈtːuːku] 'my husband'.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) closed-final lexemes with the 2SG possessive -m stressed finally ([taˈm̼am] 'your father', vs. [moˈmaːnan] 'he is ashamed' penultimate) — analysed as underlying penult via a lost suffix vowel; fn. 14 notes the alternative that closed final syllables are always stressed. (ii) final stress on the last open syllable of some disyllabic verbs in serial verb constructions ([moˈsi] 'he goes down'), 'requires further validation' (p. 259).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolation and suffixed forms). The transcribed text (p. 259) explicitly marks phrasal and sentential stress, and the authors note that not all stressed vowels lengthen and some phrase-final vowels lengthen without stress; exception (ii) is a phrase/SVC-level effect. Vowels lengthen under stress (p. 256).
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Mavea (Mav̋ea) as spoken on Mavea Island, i.e. the language Glottolog calls Mafea, mafe1237 / ISO mkv, no dialect split; speaker in the JIPA text is a female born c. 1945, one of two speakers still using linguolabials regularly. Glottolog's descriptive-reference list for mafe1237 is polluted by 'computerized assignment' false tags on unrelated works whose titles contain 'Discovering'; only the two Guérin items are real.

new_statements.reading: Mavea word stress is quantity-insensitive penultimate primary stress (non-phonemic, moves with suffixation), with secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the primary (e.g. [ˌpatuˈiːra] 'their head', [taˌmanaˈtːuːku] 'my husband'). The describers treat the closed-final-syllable cases (e.g. [taˈmʷam] 'your father') as penultimate at an underlying level via a lost possessive vowel, and record but do not adopt a reviewer's weight-based reading (closed final syllable always stressed, fn. 14); final stress on some disyllabic verbs is attributed to serial-verb-construction phrasing and flagged as needing validation. Length is not phonemic; stressed vowels lengthen (p. 256). First-hand (first author's own fieldwork 2005-2007), same describer as the 2011 UHP reference grammar whose TOC (open JCU copy) confirms the 'penultimate stress with exceptions' analysis.
